lessons.title: Same idea, different words
lessons.strategy: Harder questions do not copy the text's words. Turn the question into its idea, then look for the sentence that says the same idea in other words.
lessons.tip: Swap the question's words for words that mean the same, then search for those.

worked.prompt: How far did the women have to go to fetch water?
worked.answer: Four kilometres, to the neighbouring village.
steps: The text never says fetch water. Think of the idea: getting water from somewhere else.
Find that idea in other words: 'women walked four kilometres to the next village with pots on their heads.'
Carrying pots means fetching water, and the next village is the neighbouring one. The answer is four kilometres.

lessons.title: When the telling is out of order
lessons.strategy: A writer may begin at the end and then go back. Phrases like three summers ago, back then and until two years ago show the jump. Rebuild the real order before you answer.
lessons.tip: Sort the events into then and now. The opening lines are often the latest moment, not the earliest.

worked.prompt: Which happened first: the pump began to hum, Selvi posted her letter, or the old well dried up?
steps: The text opens with now: the pump hums all day. That is the latest moment, although it is told first.
'Three summers ago' takes us back: the well had dried up. After that Selvi wrote, the engineers came, and the pump was built.
Real order: well dries up, letter, engineers, pump. So the well drying up happened first.

lessons.title: Causes the writer leaves unsaid
lessons.strategy: Sometimes the text gives the facts and leaves you to join them. Ask what happened earlier that could have made this happen, and check that the text supports the link.
lessons.tip: Your cause must rest on something the text says. If you cannot point to a line, it is a guess.

worked.prompt: Why did engineers come to Keezhur?
worked.answer: Because of the letter Selvi sent to the district office.
steps: The text only says: 'Engineers arrived two months later.' It gives no reason.
Later than what? Selvi had posted a letter with her measurements to the district office.
Offices send engineers, and the last paragraph says one careful letter did more than years of complaining. The letter brought them.

lessons.title: Mixed and changing feelings
lessons.strategy: People can say one thing and do another, or feel differently as time passes. Put what a person says beside what they do, early and late, and describe both.
lessons.tip: If words and actions point different ways, the true feeling usually includes both.

worked.prompt: How did the uncle's view of Selvi's letter change?
worked.answer: He began by mocking it and ended with quiet respect for her.
steps: Early on he says, 'Nothing will come of it,' laughing. He does not take the letter seriously.
When the pump starts, he carries the first pot home himself and leaves a new pen on her schoolbag.
He never says sorry or well done, but a pen for the letter-writer shows respect. His view moved from mockery to quiet respect.

lessons.title: The main idea of the whole text
lessons.strategy: In a longer text, ask what each paragraph adds, then find the one idea that all the paragraphs build together. It must be bigger than any single paragraph and no wider than the text.
lessons.tip: Test each answer: too small (one detail), too big (more than the text says), or just right?

worked.prompt: What is the main idea of the whole text?
worked.answer: One girl's careful letter brought water to her village.
steps: Paragraph by paragraph: the village had no water; Selvi measured and wrote; engineers came and built the pump; the writer reflects on the letter.
'The women walked four kilometres' is true but covers only one paragraph. It is too small.
The idea that links all four paragraphs is that Selvi's careful letter brought water to the village.

lessons.title: Opinions dressed as facts
lessons.strategy: Phrases like everyone knows, it is a fact that and it is obvious make an opinion sound settled. Ignore the label and ask whether the statement itself could be checked and whether everyone would agree.
lessons.tip: Cover the opening phrase and read what is left. Could you prove it?

worked.prompt: Which sentence is an opinion presented as if it were a fact?
worked.answer: Everyone knows that villages are forgotten by offices.
steps: 'Engineers arrived two months later.' This could be checked in the office records. It is a fact.
'Everyone knows that villages are forgotten by offices.' Cover 'Everyone knows that' and read the rest: villages are forgotten by offices.
That is a sweeping judgement, and this very story shows an office that answered. The phrase everyone knows only dresses the opinion as a fact.

passages.title: The Well at Keezhur
passages.text:
The pump at the edge of Keezhur village hums all day now, and nobody stops to look at it. Three summers ago, things were different. The old well had dried up, and women walked four kilometres to the next village with pots on their heads.

Selvi, who was twelve then, used to miss the first hour of school to carry water. One morning she measured the walk with her brother's cycle meter and wrote the numbers in a letter to the district office. “Nothing will come of it,” her uncle said, laughing. Selvi posted it anyway.

Engineers arrived two months later. They found water deep under the tamarind grove, and by the next monsoon the pump was running. On the day it started, Selvi's uncle carried the first pot home himself. He did not say a word, but he left a new pen on her schoolbag.

Everyone knows that villages are forgotten by offices. Yet one careful letter did more than years of complaining. Selvi is now in Class 10, and she has not been late to school since.

passages.title: The Reading Bus
passages.text:
Today the green bus parked outside Thenur school is the busiest place in the village. A year ago it was a rusting wreck behind the depot.

Mr Subbiah had driven that bus for thirty years. When he retired, the company planned to sell it for scrap. “Give it to me instead,” he said. His wife thought he had lost his senses. “We need a new roof, not an old bus,” she told him, but she packed his lunch every morning while he scraped off the rust.

He took out the seats and built shelves. Neighbours gave books; a paint shop gave four tins of green paint. In March the bus rolled, slowly, to the school gate.

On the first day, only three children climbed in. Mr Subbiah read aloud to them anyway. By the end of the month, the teachers were sending whole classes. His wife now keeps the borrowing register, and scolds anyone who returns a book late.

It is a well-known fact that children no longer read. The crowded bus suggests otherwise. Last term its shelves held nine hundred books, and most were out on loan.

questions.prompt: What was going to happen to the bus when Mr Subbiah stopped working?
questions.right: It was going to be sold as waste metal.
wrong: It was going to be given to the school.
It was going to be painted green.
questions.evidence: the company planned to sell it for scrap
questions.explain: Stopped working means retired, and sold as waste metal means sold for scrap: 'When he retired, the company planned to sell it for scrap.'
questions.hint: 'Stopped working' is another way of saying retired. Find that sentence and put its ending in your own words.

questions.prompt: Which of these happened first?
questions.right: Mr Subbiah asked the company for the bus.
wrong: The bus stood outside the school, full of children.
Only three children climbed in.
questions.evidence: A year ago it was a rusting wreck behind the depot.
questions.explain: The text opens with today, then goes back a year. He asked for the bus when he retired, before the repairs, before the first day with three children, and long before today's busy bus.
questions.hint: The first sentence is about today. Find the words that take the story back in time.

questions.prompt: Why were most of the books not on the shelves last term?
questions.right: Children had borrowed them.
wrong: They had been sold for scrap.
The neighbours had taken them back.
questions.evidence: most were out on loan
questions.explain: 'Most were out on loan' means they had been borrowed. The text never says who borrowed them, but the crowded bus and the borrowing register tell us: the children.
questions.hint: What does 'out on loan' mean? Who uses this bus?

questions.prompt: How did Mrs Subbiah feel about the bus at the beginning?
questions.right: She thought it was foolish, but she still supported her husband.
wrong: She was proud and excited about the plan from the very first day.
She was angry and refused to help.
questions.evidence: she packed his lunch every morning while he scraped off the rust
questions.explain: Her words were against it: 'We need a new roof, not an old bus.' Her actions helped: she packed his lunch every morning. Both are true together.
questions.hint: Put what she said beside what she did every morning. Do they point the same way?

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the whole text?
questions.right: One man's patient work turned a scrap bus into a library that children love.
wrong: A paint shop gave four tins of green paint, and neighbours gave books for the shelves.
Old buses should always be sold for scrap.
questions.evidence: He took out the seats and built shelves.
questions.explain: Every paragraph builds this: the wreck, his decision, the rebuilding, the growing crowd, the books on loan. The paint is one detail, and the text never argues that buses should be scrapped.
questions.hint: Which answer fits all five paragraphs: not one detail, and not more than the text says?

questions.prompt: Which sentence is an opinion presented as if it were a fact?
questions.right: It is a well-known fact that children no longer read.
wrong: Mr Subbiah had driven that bus for thirty years.
On the first day, only three children climbed in.
questions.evidence: It is a well-known fact that children no longer read.
questions.explain: Cover 'It is a well-known fact that': 'children no longer read' is a sweeping judgement, and the crowded bus contradicts it. The other two can be checked.
questions.hint: Find a phrase that announces a fact. Cover it, and ask whether the rest could be proved.

passages.title: The Kabaddi Cup
passages.text:
The cup stands on a shelf in the staff room of Vaigai Girls' School, and the players touch it for luck before every match. Nobody would have believed that last November.

Back then the team had lost eleven games in a row. Their coach, Ms Devi, had been told the ground would be given to the boys' cricket team unless results improved. She said nothing to the girls. Instead, she moved practice to six in the morning and filmed every session on her phone.

“She is punishing us,” Pavithra, the captain, complained to her mother. Yet she was the first to arrive each dawn, and she watched the videos twice. In them she saw what the coach had seen: the team scattered whenever a raider crossed the line.

They practised holding the chain for six weeks. In the district final, the chain held for the whole second half, and Vaigai won by four points. Pavithra handed the cup to Ms Devi and could not get her words out.

Everyone agrees that talent wins matches. This team had no stars at all. What it had was a coach who looked closely and girls who came back each morning.

questions.prompt: How badly had the team been doing before the change?
questions.right: It had been beaten in eleven matches one after another.
wrong: It had lost the district final by four points in the second half.
It had lost six matches in six weeks.
questions.evidence: the team had lost eleven games in a row
questions.explain: Beaten in eleven matches one after another says the same as 'had lost eleven games in a row'. Four points and six weeks belong to other sentences.
questions.hint: The question says 'how badly'. Look for the sentence about losing, and match its meaning, not its words.

questions.prompt: Which of these happened last?
questions.right: The players began touching the cup for luck before matches.
wrong: Vaigai won the district final.
Ms Devi moved practice to six in the morning and filmed it.
questions.evidence: the players touch it for luck before every match
questions.explain: The first paragraph describes now, after everything else. They can only touch the cup because they won it, and they won it after the early practices.
questions.hint: The opening lines describe the present. Is the present the earliest or the latest moment in this story?

questions.prompt: Why did Ms Devi change the way the team practised?
questions.right: She feared the team would lose its ground unless it started winning.
wrong: She wanted to punish the girls for losing.
The boys' cricket team had asked to use the ground in the evenings.
questions.evidence: the ground would be given to the boys' cricket team unless results improved
questions.explain: She had been told the ground would go unless results improved, and then she changed the practice. Punishment is only Pavithra's complaint, not the coach's reason.
questions.hint: What had the coach been told just before she changed the practice time?

questions.prompt: How did Pavithra feel about the early practices?
questions.right: She grumbled about them, but she was fully committed.
wrong: She hated them and tried to avoid them whenever she could.
She enjoyed them and never complained.
questions.evidence: Yet she was the first to arrive each dawn, and she watched the videos twice.
questions.explain: She complained that the coach was punishing them, yet she arrived first each dawn and watched the videos twice. Complaint and commitment sit side by side.
questions.hint: Compare what Pavithra told her mother with what she did each dawn.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the whole text?
questions.right: Careful coaching and steady effort, not star players, turned a losing team into champions.
wrong: The cup is kept on a shelf in the staff room, and the players touch it for luck before every match.
Kabaddi teams deserve better grounds than cricket teams.
questions.evidence: What it had was a coach who looked closely and girls who came back each morning.
questions.explain: The losing run, the filmed practices, the six weeks of work and the final all build to the last paragraph's point. The shelf is a detail, and the text does not compare the two sports.
questions.hint: Read the last paragraph again. Which answer says what the whole story was building towards?

questions.prompt: Which sentence is an opinion presented as if it were a fact?
questions.right: Everyone agrees that talent wins matches.
wrong: Vaigai won by four points.
Back then the team had lost eleven games in a row.
questions.evidence: Everyone agrees that talent wins matches.
questions.explain: 'Everyone agrees' makes a judgement sound settled, and the story itself argues against it. The scores and the losses could be checked.
questions.hint: Which sentence claims that everybody thinks the same? Could that be proved?

passages.title: The Stepwell
passages.text:
Tourists now photograph the stepwell at Arasur every weekend, and a guide in a blue cap tells its story. Until two years ago, the same well was a rubbish pit that people hurried past.

The change began with a history lesson. Karthik's teacher showed the class a faded picture of the well from 1920, with clear water and carved pillars. Karthik lived three streets away and had never known it was there. That evening he climbed down as far as the plastic bags allowed and counted nineteen carved steps.

“It is a job for the government,” his father said. “Besides, your exams are near.” But on Sunday his father arrived with two spades and a flask of tea. Thirty neighbours joined over the following months. The last of the rubbish was carried out in a tractor just before the rains, and the well filled for the first time in forty years.

It is common knowledge that young people do not care about old things. The guide in the blue cap is Karthik, who is fifteen. He gives the tour money to the school history club.

questions.prompt: What did the well look like in the old photograph?
questions.right: It had clean water and decorated columns.
wrong: It was full of plastic bags.
It had nineteen broken steps under the water.
questions.evidence: with clear water and carved pillars
questions.explain: Clean water and decorated columns say the same as 'clear water and carved pillars'. The plastic bags are from Karthik's own visit.

questions.prompt: Which of these happened first?
questions.right: A teacher showed the class an old picture of the well.
wrong: A guide in a blue cap began telling the well's story to tourists.
A tractor carried out the last of the rubbish.
questions.evidence: The change began with a history lesson.
questions.explain: The text opens with the present, then goes back: the lesson came first, the clean-up followed, and the tourists and the guide came last.

questions.prompt: Why had Karthik never noticed the well, although he lived close by?
questions.right: It was buried in rubbish and people ignored it.
wrong: It was locked behind a gate in another street.
It had been built only recently.
questions.evidence: the same well was a rubbish pit that people hurried past
questions.explain: The text does not give the reason directly, but it says the well was a rubbish pit that people hurried past. Nothing about it looked worth noticing.

questions.prompt: What did Karthik's father really feel about the clean-up?
questions.right: He raised objections, but he cared enough to help.
wrong: He thought it was a waste of time and stayed away.
He was eager from the first moment.
questions.evidence: But on Sunday his father arrived with two spades and a flask of tea.
questions.explain: His words were objections: the government's job, the exams. His actions were help: two spades and a flask of tea. Both belong in the answer.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the whole text?
questions.right: A boy's curiosity led a neighbourhood to bring a forgotten well back to life.
wrong: The well has nineteen carved steps.
The government, not the neighbours, should clean every old well in the country.
questions.evidence: Thirty neighbours joined over the following months.
questions.explain: The lesson, Karthik's visit, the neighbours' work and the well today all build this idea. The steps are a detail, and the text makes no demand of the government.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is an opinion presented as if it were a fact?
questions.right: It is common knowledge that young people do not care about old things.
wrong: Thirty neighbours joined over the following months.
The guide in the blue cap is Karthik, who is fifteen.
questions.evidence: It is common knowledge that young people do not care about old things.
questions.explain: 'It is common knowledge' dresses up a sweeping judgement, and Karthik's story contradicts it. The other two can be checked.

passages.title: The Lamp Maker
passages.text:
The fishing boats of Mullai beach go out at four in the morning, and each one now carries a small white lamp that needs no kerosene. The lamps were built by a girl who is afraid of the sea.

Jenifa's fear began when she was nine. Her father's boat came back one night without its lantern, which had tipped over and set a net alight. No one was hurt, but she did not sleep properly for weeks.

At thirteen she joined an electronics club in town. Her first solar lamp took four months and failed twice in salt air. “Leave it, kanna,” her father told her. “We have managed with kerosene for fifty years.” He said this while holding the torch for her as she soldered.

The third lamp survived a full month at sea. After that, other fishermen began knocking at the door. Jenifa has now made sixty lamps, and she still refuses to step into a boat.

Everybody knows that inventors are fearless people. Jenifa says her lamp exists only because she was frightened.

questions.prompt: What went wrong on the night Jenifa's fear began?
questions.right: A lantern fell over and a net caught fire.
wrong: Her father's boat sank.
A solar lamp failed twice in the salt air.
questions.evidence: which had tipped over and set a net alight
questions.explain: Fell over and caught fire say the same as 'tipped over and set a net alight'. The boat came back, and the solar lamps came years later.

questions.prompt: Which of these happened first?
questions.right: Her father's boat returned without its lantern.
wrong: Jenifa joined an electronics club.
Other fishermen began knocking at the door for lamps.
questions.evidence: Jenifa's fear began when she was nine.
questions.explain: The text opens with the present, then goes back to when she was nine. The club came at thirteen and the fishermen came after the third lamp.

questions.prompt: Why did other fishermen begin knocking at the door?
questions.right: They had seen that the lamp worked at sea and wanted one.
wrong: They wanted to complain that the bright light scared the fish.
They were selling kerosene.
questions.evidence: The third lamp survived a full month at sea.
questions.explain: The reason is not stated, but the knocking came just after the lamp lasted a month at sea, and Jenifa went on to make sixty lamps. They wanted lamps of their own.

questions.prompt: How did Jenifa's father feel about her lamp-making?
questions.right: He doubted it aloud, but he quietly supported her.
wrong: He was against it and would not help.
He was sure from the very start that the lamp would work.
questions.evidence: He said this while holding the torch for her as she soldered.
questions.explain: He told her to leave it, yet he held the torch for her while she worked. His words doubted and his hands helped.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the whole text?
questions.right: A girl's fear of the sea led her to invent a lamp the fishing boats now use.
wrong: Solar lamps often fail in salt air, so fishermen have kept kerosene for fifty years.
Jenifa joined an electronics club at thirteen.
questions.evidence: Jenifa says her lamp exists only because she was frightened.
questions.explain: Her fear, the failed attempts, the working lamp and the boats today all build this idea. The other answers are single details.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is an opinion presented as if it were a fact?
questions.right: Everybody knows that inventors are fearless people.
wrong: Jenifa has now made sixty lamps, and she still refuses to step into a boat.
The third lamp survived a full month at sea.
questions.evidence: Everybody knows that inventors are fearless people.
questions.explain: 'Everybody knows' makes a judgement sound settled, and Jenifa herself is an inventor who is afraid. The other two can be checked.

passages.title: The Corner Table
passages.text:
At Murugan's tea shop in Tirunelveli, the corner table is kept free after five o'clock, and nobody dares put a glass on it. It belongs to the chess club.

The club is the work of Mrs Kamala, a retired bank clerk. She first came to the shop four winters ago, simply to escape her silent flat. She brought a folding board and played against herself. Murugan disliked it. “People who sit for two hours and buy one tea are bad for business,” he muttered.

A schoolboy stopped to watch, then a lorry driver. Within a year there were twenty players, and the shop sold more tea in the evenings than in the mornings. Murugan put up a shelf for the boards with his own hands.

Last month, two of the children Mrs Kamala taught reached the state finals. She watched from the back row, twisting her handkerchief.

It is obvious that clubs need money and halls to succeed. This one began with a lonely woman, a folding board and one cup of tea.

questions.prompt: What first brought Mrs Kamala to the tea shop?
questions.right: She wanted to get away from her quiet, empty home.
wrong: She wanted to start a chess club.
She wanted to train children for the state finals.
questions.evidence: simply to escape her silent flat
questions.explain: Get away from her quiet home says the same as 'escape her silent flat'. The club and the finals came later and were not her reason for coming.

questions.prompt: Which of these happened last?
questions.right: Two of her pupils reached the state finals.
wrong: Murugan put up a shelf for the boards himself.
A lorry driver stopped to watch.
questions.evidence: Last month, two of the children Mrs Kamala taught reached the state finals.
questions.explain: The watchers came first, the shelf came once the club had grown, and the state finals were only last month.

questions.prompt: Why did the shop begin to sell more tea in the evenings?
questions.right: The chess players filled the shop in the evenings.
wrong: Murugan lowered the price of tea after five o'clock.
The shop was closed in the mornings.
questions.evidence: Within a year there were twenty players
questions.explain: The text puts the twenty players and the evening tea sales in one sentence and leaves the link to the reader: more people in the shop meant more tea sold.

questions.prompt: How did Murugan's attitude to the chess players change?
questions.right: He moved from annoyance to proud support.
wrong: He welcomed them warmly from the first day.
He stayed annoyed and wanted them to leave.
questions.evidence: Murugan put up a shelf for the boards with his own hands.
questions.explain: At first he muttered that such customers were bad for business. Later he built a shelf for the boards with his own hands. His feeling changed.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the whole text?
questions.right: One lonely woman's habit grew into a chess club that changed a tea shop.
wrong: Murugan's tea shop now sells more tea in the evenings than it does in the mornings.
Every chess club should meet in a tea shop.
questions.evidence: This one began with a lonely woman, a folding board and one cup of tea.
questions.explain: Her arrival, the growing circle, Murugan's shelf and the state finals all build this idea. The tea sales are one detail, and the text gives no rule for other clubs.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is an opinion presented as if it were a fact?
questions.right: It is obvious that clubs need money and halls to succeed.
wrong: Within a year there were twenty players, and the shop sold more tea in the evenings than in the mornings.
The club is the work of Mrs Kamala, a retired bank clerk.
questions.evidence: It is obvious that clubs need money and halls to succeed.
questions.explain: 'It is obvious' dresses up a judgement, and this club succeeded with neither money nor a hall. The other two can be checked.

passages.title: The Radio School
passages.text:
Every weekday at eleven, forty radios across the Kolli hills are tuned to the same station, and children sit beneath them with notebooks open. The teacher they are listening to has never met most of them.

Mr Ilango started the broadcasts during the floods of 2021, when the hill roads were cut for nine weeks. He had taught in the valley school for twenty years, and he could not bear the thought of his pupils forgetting their sums. He borrowed a transmitter from the forest office and read lessons into it from his kitchen.

The head teacher was not pleased. “A school is a building, Ilango,” she told him. Still, she was the one who drove up the broken road with a sack of batteries when the first radios went quiet.

When the roads reopened, the pupils came back able to do long division. The broadcasts were meant to stop then. Parents from hamlets with no school at all asked for them to go on, and they have.

It is a plain fact that real teaching needs a classroom. Forty radios disagree.

questions.prompt: Where did Mr Ilango give his first radio lessons from?
questions.right: from his own home
wrong: from the forest office
from the valley school
questions.evidence: read lessons into it from his kitchen
questions.explain: His kitchen is in his own home. The forest office only lent the transmitter, and the valley school is where he used to teach.

questions.prompt: Which of these happened first?
questions.right: Floods cut the hill roads.
wrong: Parents from the hamlets asked for the lessons to go on.
The head teacher brought a sack of batteries.
questions.evidence: during the floods of 2021, when the hill roads were cut for nine weeks
questions.explain: The text opens with the present, then goes back to the floods. The batteries came during the broadcasts, and the parents asked after the roads reopened.

questions.prompt: Why did the first radios go quiet?
questions.right: Their batteries had run out.
wrong: The transmitter was returned to the forest office.
The floods washed the radios away.
questions.evidence: with a sack of batteries when the first radios went quiet
questions.explain: The text never says why, but the head teacher answered the silence with a sack of batteries. The radios had run out of power.

questions.prompt: Why did Mr Ilango begin the broadcasts?
questions.right: He worried that his cut-off pupils would fall behind.
wrong: He wanted to become well known across the hills on the radio.
The head teacher ordered him to.
questions.evidence: he could not bear the thought of his pupils forgetting their sums
questions.explain: He could not bear the thought of his pupils forgetting their sums while the roads were cut. The head teacher was against the idea, so she did not order it.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the whole text?
questions.right: Radio lessons begun in an emergency became a lasting school for hill children.
wrong: The hill roads were closed for nine weeks.
Radios are better than classrooms for every child, in the hills and in the valley.
questions.evidence: Parents from hamlets with no school at all asked for them to go on, and they have.
questions.explain: The floods, the kitchen lessons, the batteries and the hamlets that kept the broadcasts all build this idea. Nine weeks is a detail, and the text does not claim radios are better for everyone.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is an opinion presented as if it were a fact?
questions.right: It is a plain fact that real teaching needs a classroom.
wrong: He borrowed a transmitter from the forest office and read lessons into it from his kitchen.
The broadcasts were meant to stop then.
questions.evidence: It is a plain fact that real teaching needs a classroom.
questions.explain: Calling something a plain fact does not make it one. This is a judgement, and the forty radios in the story argue against it.
